conflict_topics: access to stove (blocked by unwashed pan)
use of extractor fan and closing the kitchen door
dialogue_quality_notes: Conversation is concise and practical; participants state concrete complaints and quickly move to a simple rule.
Two related but distinct issues (smell and unwashed pan) are handled in parallel, which is efficient.
Little needless repetition; most turns advance the problem or propose a solution.
evaluation.final_reason: The group agreed concrete behavioral rules: Agent C proposed "agree to wash whatever we use as soon as we're done cooking," D accepted ("Sounds good to me"), and Agent A explicitly accepted: "Fine. We wash our own things. And I can close the door." This mutual acceptance settled both the cleaning and smell-mitigation demands.
position_change_notes: Agent A moved from defensive (noting they'd finished and claiming they used the fan) to explicit acceptance: "Fine. We wash our own things. And I can close the door."
Agent C advanced from complaint to proposing a concrete household rule (wash as soon as done) and remained consistent.
Agent D shifted from complaint to endorsing the proposed rule ("Sounds good to me").
Agent B introduced the smell concern and requested mitigations (fan use, close door); B's request was accepted as part of the final compromise.

round_scores.evidence: Agent D: "By the time I get home, the kitchen's always a mess or someone's using it. I just want to cook." vs Agent A: "I just finished. But the pan from last night is still there." — a clear dispute over kitchen state and use.
Agent D: "Right, and I can't use the pan. So I still can't cook." and Agent A: "Well, it needs to be washed." — the same practical incompatibility (access to pan/stove) persists without resolution.

Agent B raises a new but related issue: "The smell is the problem... Can you please use the fan and close the door when you're cooking?" Agent A replies defensively: "I was using the fan." — introduces a second substantive complaint (smell mitigation) and disagreement about whether current behavior suffices.

Agent B: "The fan's not enough then. It's still really strong. Can you shut the kitchen door as well next time?" and Agent C: "But nobody can use the stove until this pan is washed." — stronger opposing positions (a demand to change cooking behavior and an insistence that the unwashed pan prevents others from cooking).

Agent D: "Exactly." (supports C). Agent C proposes a concrete rule: "So, can we just agree to wash whatever we use as soon as we're done cooking?" — moves toward resolution but not yet accepted by all (A has not agreed yet).
Agent D: "Sounds good to me." and Agent A: "Fine. We wash our own things. And I can close the door." — explicit mutual acceptance of the proposed practical arrangements.

substantive_insights: The conflict involved two linked practical problems: a persistent smell nuisance and a shared unwashed pan that blocks stove use.
Majority alignment (B, C, D) applied pressure toward a shared-norm solution; a direct proposal from C produced a focal solution.
Resolution is pragmatic and behavioral (wash your own items; close the door) but contains no enforcement or follow-up mechanism.
